props.title: Piranha
props.initialSlug: Killer fish terrorize summer lake resort paradise

sections.content: Piranha (1978) launched Joe Dante's career with a perfect B-movie blend of horror and humor. Producer Roger Corman clearly aimed to capitalize on Jaws (1975), but Dante and screenwriter John Sayles crafted something uniquely entertaining. The film's genius lies in its self-aware approach - mixing genuine scares with satirical jabs at military experiments and summer resort culture. While Jaws used minimal shark footage, Piranha gleefully shows its mutant fish swarms, embracing practical effects that still hold up surprisingly well. The film established Dante's signature style of mixing horror with dark comedy, which he'd later perfect in Gremlins (1984).

sections.content: The late 1970s saw an explosion of aquatic horror following Jaws' success. While most were straightforward copycats, the cleverer entries found unique angles. Deep Rising (1998) added tentacled monsters and a heist plot, while Crawling Eye (1978) went the prehistoric route. Orca (1977) attempted a more serious approach, positioning itself as the "thinking person's Jaws" with themes of revenge and intelligence in nature. But Piranha's knowing wit set it apart, influencing later horror-comedies like Tremors (1990). SUBHEAD: The Evolution of Aquatic Horror

Modern aquatic horror has largely abandoned Piranha's practical effects charm for CGI spectacle. Deep Blue Sea (1999) super-sized its sharks while adding genetic engineering themes. Alexandre Aja's Piranha 3D (2010) remake amped up the gore and exploitation elements to deliberately excessive levels. Yet the original Piranha's influence surfaces in films like The Host (2006), which similarly blends creature feature thrills with social commentary and humor.
